                    ### Question
                    A 21-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 2-week history of progressive shortness of breath and intermittent cough with blood-tinged sputum. During this time, he has also noticed blood in his urine. He has no history of serious illness and does not take any medications. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 152/90 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows crackles at both lung bases. Urinalysis is positive for blood and results of a direct enzyme-linked immunoassay are positive for anti-GBM antibodies. The pathogenesis of this patient's disease is most similar to which of the following?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Henoch-Schönlein purpura
opb. Polyarteritis nodosa
opc. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis
opd. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia
ope. Graft versus host disease

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's presentation of pulmonary symptoms and renal involvement with positive anti-GBM antibodies strongly indicates Goodpasture syndrome. This autoimmune condition targets the basement membrane in both the kidneys and lungs, leading to glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage. This pathogenesis is distinct from other conditions such as Polyarteritis nodosa, which involves systemic vasculitis but not through anti-GBM antibodies, and Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, which is mediated by immune complexes rather than direct autoimmune attack.
